title: Uncertainty-Aware Diagnostics for Physics-Informed Machine Learning
one_liner: Choose physics-informed model settings with one evidence score that balances data fit and physical consistency through uncertainty, instead of trusting several losses that can disagree.
lead: Physics-informed learning mixes two sources of supervision: observed data and physical laws such as differential equations. A model can appear strong on one loss and weak on the other, which makes hyperparameter selection hard. This paper introduces the Physics-Informed Log Evidence score, or PILE, inside a Gaussian process setting. The score uses uncertainty to judge whether a model setting explains both the data and the physical constraint well enough at the same time.

problem.h2: Two training objectives can point to different models
paras: A physics-informed model is usually trained to fit observed data and also satisfy a physical equation. Those two goals can pull in different directions. One model setting may fit the data closely but violate the equation, while another may satisfy the equation but miss the observed values.

Because of that tension, common selection rules are ambiguous. Looking only at test error can hide a bad physical fit, while looking only at equation residuals can hide a poor data fit. The deeper issue is that these raw losses do not tell you whether the model's uncertainty makes the tradeoff acceptable.

callout.html: Physics-informed tuning is hard because data loss and physics loss can disagree, and raw loss values do not say whether the model is uncertain in the right places.

steps.b: Step 1: Define a Gaussian process model.
steps.text: Use a Gaussian process, which means a probabilistic function model with a mean and covariance rule, so predictions come with uncertainty.
Translate the governing differential equation into the model's covariance structure and residual calculations.
Evaluate how plausible the observed data and the physics-consistent function values are under one model setting.

steps.b: Step 4: Compare settings such as bandwidth, penalty strength, or compute routine choice.
steps.text: Rank candidate settings by the same evidence score instead of by several separate losses.

steps.b: Step 5: Choose the setting with the best score.
steps.text: Use that one setting for training or for data acquisition planning.

paras: The paper changes the model-selection rule. It replaces several competing loss numbers with one uncertainty-aware evidence score for choosing hyperparameters.
object.object: the criterion used to choose model settings

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: whether the uncertainty is believable
hidden.name: joint plausibility of data and physics under the model
paras: A low loss can still be misleading if the model is confident in the wrong places or uncertain in the wrong places. The missing quantity is whether the whole model setting makes the observed data and the physics constraint jointly plausible under its own uncertainty assumptions.

PILE measures that plausibility. A setting scores well only if it fits the data and the physical rule in a way the model itself considers believable. That is why the score can reject settings that look good under one raw loss but are poorly calibrated overall.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark settings that win on one view but fail once data, physics, and uncertainty are judged together.

reads.html: The hidden question is whether the model's own uncertainty makes its story believable. PILE scores that directly.
PILE uses log evidence to rank hyperparameters by the joint plausibility of observations and physics-informed structure under the Gaussian process model.

mechanism.h2: Why one evidence score beats raw loss juggling
paras: Raw losses treat all errors as point values. They do not ask whether the model claimed to be certain or uncertain in those regions. A probabilistic score does ask that question.

PILE works because it rewards settings that place high probability on the observed data while also respecting the physics-informed structure. If a setting fits the data only by becoming implausibly certain, or satisfies the equation only by giving up data fit, the evidence score falls. That single score therefore captures the tradeoff that separate losses leave unresolved.

stages.s: build Gaussian process with one candidate setting
score joint plausibility of data and physics

math.h2: The equation: choose the setting with the best log evidence
math.words: PILE assigns each candidate setting one log-evidence score, and the chosen setting is the one that maximizes that score.
math.equation: best_setting = argmax over candidate settings of log_evidence(data, physics | setting)
symbols: possible choices such as bandwidth, penalty strength, or covariance rule
the uncertainty-aware score for how plausible the observed data and physics information are under one setting
the hyperparameter choice selected by PILE

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Setting A has log-evidence score minus 12.
Setting B has log-evidence score minus 7.
Setting C has log-evidence score minus 10.
Because minus 7 is the largest of these three values, PILE selects setting B.
A lower data loss alone would not be enough to win if the uncertainty pattern made the overall model less plausible.

math.note: The Gaussian process machinery gives this score a closed probabilistic meaning: it is not just another weighted sum of losses.

charts.title: Separate loss tuning
charts.note: Several losses can disagree, so model selection becomes unstable.

charts.title: PILE-based tuning
charts.note: One evidence score ranks settings consistently because it evaluates fit and uncertainty together.

items.html: If the Gaussian process assumptions are badly mismatched to the real system, the evidence score can still rank settings poorly because the score trusts the wrong model family.
If the physical constraint is wrong or too weakly enforced in the covariance structure, PILE can favor settings that solve the wrong problem well.

items.b: Too little data to disambiguate settings.
items.html: When observations are extremely sparse, several settings can remain similarly plausible, so the score may not separate them strongly.
Use PILE when the Gaussian process model and the encoded physics rule are credible, and compare settings across a well-designed candidate range.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a one-dimensional differential-equation regression task with sparse observations. Fit several Gaussian process models that vary in bandwidth, penalty weight, and covariance rule. Rank them once by raw test loss and once by PILE.

The demo should then evaluate which ranking better predicts future physical consistency and predictive quality on held-out regions, because the paper's claim is that PILE is a better model-selection rule, not just another training loss.
demo.metric_eq: selection_success = fraction of tasks where the chosen setting is near the best held-out predictive and physics-consistency score
demo.closing: A convincing demo shows that PILE chooses settings more reliably because it judges data fit and physics fit through a single uncertainty-aware score.
